description: a student and a graduate teamed up looking for more like minded people.
summary: VITALIS is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on missions beyond low Earth orbit, where distance and communication delays make real-time ground support unreliable. Our concept pairs a phone-sized device worn on the forearm, which captures the astronaut's vital signs, with software that learns each person's own baseline (heart rate, HRV, breathing rate, SpO2, blood pressure, temperature) and flags deviations as green, amber or red. When the link with Earth or the station is lost, an on-board AI assistant explains each alert in plain language and tells the crew member what to do next, running entirely from a local database. Holm-Bonferroni correction keeps simultaneous tests from inflating false alarms (about 26.5% uncorrected versus a nominal 5%), and NOAA GOES proton data adds space-weather context. VITALIS is decision support, not diagnosis: the current build runs on simulated signals, the wearable is a design concept, and we state clearly what is implemented, designed and still to be validated.
details:
What it does / how it works. VITALIS is a decision-support app for astronauts, not a diagnostic tool. It shows live ECG, pulse and breathing waveforms, and tracks heart rate, HRV, SpO2, temperature, breathing rate and blood pressure against each person’s own baseline. It also tracks radiation dose rate, accumulated dose and live proton flux from NOAA’s GOES satellites. GOES data is used as space-weather context, not as a measure of individual dose. Each reading gets a green, amber or red status, with step-by-step guidance written for non-doctors. A rule engine separates sensor faults (such as a loose electrode) from real physiological change, so a faulty sensor doesn’t trigger a false abort. There is also a daily mood and sleep check-in and an “Analyze my data” insights function. Our hardware concept is a phone-sized device worn on the forearm that reads the astronaut's vital signs and shows this interface on the arm. If the link with Earth or the station is lost, the on-board AI assistant keeps working offline and tells the crew member what to do next.

Benefits and intended impact. Crews get more medical autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed or lost. The system runs offline from local SQLite storage, and the optional AI model only receives aggregated statistics, never raw readings. We want to make health monitoring on long missions more reliable, understandable and personal. The same approach could support remote clinics on Earth.

Tools and technologies. The backend is Python 3.11+ with FastAPI, uvicorn, SQLite and WebSocket. The frontend is TypeScript with Vite. Integrations include NOAA GOES data, ElevenLabs voice alerts (with a browser speech fallback), and optional Claude via the Anthropic API or AWS Bedrock. A simulator with five scenarios (nominal, solar particle event, hypoxia, loose electrode, fatigue) generates the signals. No physical hardware is used yet, but the simulator sits behind the same interface a Bluetooth or serial sensor would use.

Creativity. VITALIS uses personal baselines instead of fixed population thresholds. It applies Holm-Bonferroni correction across six simultaneous tests, which holds the nominal false-alarm rate at 5% per evaluation instead of about 26.5% uncorrected. It tells real physiological change apart from sensor faults and radiation hits. Alerts are also spoken aloud, and the interface is trilingual (Spanish, English, French).

Factors the team considered.

  • Offline-first operation, with the language model optional and off by default.
  • Privacy and cost controls (a spend cap, one call per 30 seconds, a character cap on speech).
  • Honest limits: all data is simulated, the medical AI path is a template using a mock provider, and translation is partial.
  • Validation in stages: test benches, terrestrial analogs and medical review.
